URL: https://www.bytebase.com/blog/what-is-new-in-postgres-18
# What's New in PostgreSQL 18: A DBA's Perspective. This post is maintained by Bytebase, an open-source database DevSecOps tool that can manage PostgreSQL. We will constantly update this post to include the latest Postgres 18.x releases. PostgreSQL 18 ships on September 25, 2025. The release moves on async I/O, UUIDv7, and a set of long-requested operational fixes — adding `NOT NULL` without a full table scan, virtual generated columns, `RETURNING` with `old`/`new` aliases, and a faster `pg_upgrade` path. * **PostgreSQL 18 Beta 1**: May 8, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 Beta 2**: July 17, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 Beta 3**: August 14, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 RC 1**: September 4, 2025. * **PostgreSQL 18 Official Release**: September 25, 2025. PostgreSQL 18 introduces an asynchronous I/O subsystem, selected by the new `io_method` server variable. **DBA Note:** Adding a `NOT NULL` on a multi-terabyte table no longer requires an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration of the scan.

---

[2] PostgreSQL: Release Notes
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0
* An asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem that can improve performance of sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, vacuums, and other operations. * pg\_upgrade now retains optimizer statistics. * Support for "skip scan" lookups that allow using multicolumn B-tree indexes in more cases. This is now the default for generated columns. * `OLD` and `NEW` support for `RETURNING` clauses in INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE commands. The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 18 are explained in more detail in the sections below. A dump/restore using pg\_dumpall or use of pg\_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option `--no-data-checksums`. The previous behavior can be performed by using the new `ONLY` option. If a `GROUP BY` clause includes all columns of a unique index, as well as other columns of the same table, those other columns are redundant and can be dropped from the grouping.

content.text:
PostgreSQL 18 was officially released on September 25, 2025.

The full feature list is broad, but since we're in the "indexes and query performance" node, let me flag the one that's most relevant to you here, then give you the rest quickly.

The headline item for our topic is skip scan on multicolumn B-tree indexes. Previously, if you had an index on `(a, b)` and your query filtered only on `b` (no `=` condition on `a`), Postgres couldn't use that index efficiently. In 18, it can "skip" through the distinct values of the leading column and still use the index. That directly changes how you think about column ordering in composite indexes — more on that if you want.

Other performance-relevant ones:
- Asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem — up to 2-3x faster sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, and vacuums on read-heavy workloads.
- `pg_upgrade` now retains optimizer statistics, so the planner makes good decisions immediately after an upgrade instead of needing a fresh `ANALYZE`.
- `EXPLAIN` now shows buffer usage by default, which makes diagnosing slow queries easier.

The rest are less about query performance (out of our scope here) — UUIDv7, virtual generated columns, `OLD`/`NEW` in `RETURNING`, OAuth 2.0 auth, temporal constraints, parallel streaming for replication.

Want me to go deeper on skip scan and what it means for how you design composite indexes? That's squarely in our territory and it's probably the most practically useful thing in this release for you.
